episode_title: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes

stories.topic: The Doctor Who Couldn't Say What He Knew
stories.summary: Diagnosed at HbA1c 7.7 with type 2 diabetes and hypertension, Amit was prescribed metformin and the standard cocktail. When he asked about diet, the doctor looked embarrassed. In that pause Amit sensed the doctor knew everything he had been taught was wrong, but couldn't say so. Instead: 'You're a smart man, you know what to do.'
stories.insight: A whole regime of bad nutrition advice persists because individual practitioners can't openly contradict the institutions that trained them. The most honest thing a doctor can do is sometimes a meaningful look — and a curious patient is the only one who can act on it.

stories.topic: Five Years of Poker, 105 kg, and the COVID Relapse
stories.summary: Amit played professional poker for five years — 15-hour sessions, sleep, repeat — and ballooned to 105 kg. Five years before the diagnosis, he discovered the science of sugar, did keto plus intermittent fasting plus daily running, dropped to 85-86 kg, even ran 10ks, and held that weight for years. Then COVID came, he sat in a chair all day, comfort-ate biryani and pizza, climbed to 107 kg, and was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. He went back on keto with a CGM, progressed to one-meal-a-day, and reversed his HbA1c from 7.7 to 5.7.
stories.insight: Sustainable health is not a one-time achievement; it is a fragile equilibrium that life events can shatter. The same protocol that worked the first time will work the second — but you have to notice the slide early, ideally with a tool that doesn't lie.

stories.topic: The Friend Who Swore By Oats
stories.summary: A friend of Amit's would not let go of the belief that oats are healthy; every time he cited studies she dismissed him as crazy. Eventually she put on a CGM. Oats took her glucose to 280. The next day, eggs flatlined. She wore the CGM for a month, overhauled her lifestyle, and dropped 25 kg.
stories.insight: Argument loses to evidence-on-your-own-skin. Conventional wisdom about food collapses the moment a person sees their own body's response in real time — which is why personalized data is doing what decades of nutrition writing couldn't.

stories.summary: After climbing above Dharamshala, Ajay ate at the summit a meal of white rice, rajma, and a 500ml bottle of Gatorade, then immediately descended 1,000 metres on foot. Wearing a CGM, he watched the textbook play out in real time: first a sugar spike from the Gatorade, burned out by the descent; then a delayed spike as amylase converted the white rice; finally a slow, third spike as the rajma's complex carbs reached the blood. In ordinary life on the plains the three would have merged into an indistinct smear.
stories.insight: The reason food science is so hard is that the human body normally serves up smeared, overlapping signals. Strip away the noise (high energy outgo, an empty stomach, a CGM) and the textbook becomes vivid and the causal connections obvious. Knowledge needs the right experimental conditions, even on yourself.

stories.topic: Ajay Made Sonhita Cry — And She Kept Coming Back
stories.summary: Sonhita, a former colleague who worked under Ajay at NIPFP for four years, told Amit Ajay was 'horrible to work with — a monster' who would make her cry, often. But she said the same thing the others did: 'I learned so much with him,' and she kept coming back.
stories.insight: High-standards mentorship is awful in the moment and transformative in retrospect. The best teachers are often the ones whose students cry — and return.

stories.topic: The Chess Rating That Tracks His Diet
stories.summary: Amit plays a lot of bullet chess on chess.com under a pseudonym, purely as an addict — not to improve. So his rating is a stable baseline that drifts only with his cognition. On keto he's up 150 points. Eat a pizza on a cheat day and the rating drops 150. Add a biryani on top of the pizza and it drops more.
stories.insight: Brain fog is real and measurable if you have the right instrument. A consistent activity you do daily — chess, writing, running — is a personal cognition meter. Use it.

recommendations.creator: Gary Taubes
recommendations.context: An award-winning science journalist's most overarching book on sugar — described by Michael Pollan as written by 'a Solzhenitsyn of the nutrition world.'
recommendations.reason: Argues that sugars (sucrose, high-fructose corn syrup) are fundamental causes of diabetes and obesity 'using the same simple concept of causality we employ when we say smoking causes lung cancer' — not because we eat too much, but because of unique hormonal effects. The book also documents the institutional capture of nutrition science by the sugar lobby.

recommendations.creator: Nina Teicholz
recommendations.context: A journalistic exposé of how a half-century of low-fat dogma was built on cherry-picked studies.
recommendations.reason: Demolishes the saturated-fat-causes-heart-disease consensus and traces the dogma back to Ancel Keys's Seven Countries Study and the lobbying that protected it. Essential to understanding why the conventional dietary wisdom you grew up with is wrong.

recommendations.creator: Jason Fung
recommendations.context: Fung's framework for obesity as a hormonal — not caloric — disorder.
recommendations.reason: Reframes weight as a function of insulin and other hormones rather than calorie arithmetic, and lays out fasting as a tool to bring those hormones back under control.

recommendations.creator: Jason Fung
recommendations.context: Companion to The Obesity Code, focused on type 2 diabetes.
recommendations.reason: The book Amit kept gifting friends years before he acted on it himself. The practical playbook for reversing type 2 diabetes through diet and fasting — 'any doctor who tells you type 2 diabetes is a chronic disease and cannot be reversed is a lying quack.'

recommendations.creator: Sidney Mintz
recommendations.context: An anthropological history of sugar.
recommendations.reason: Provides the cultural and historical grounding — including the line that 'highly refined sucrose produces peculiar physiological effects,' and the tradition of sugar's first taste being an 'astonishment, a kind of intoxication.'

recommendations.creator: Michael Pollan
recommendations.context: Pollan's exploration of plants that have shaped human desire — apples, tulips, cannabis, the potato — and the reciprocal relationship between us.
recommendations.reason: Source of the unforgettable account of Pollan's son Isaac's first taste of sugar at his birthday cake — an 'ecstasy in the literal sense' that he was 'beside himself with the pleasure of, no longer here with me in space and time.'

recommendations.item: Nina Teicholz on The Joe Rogan Experience
recommendations.creator: Joe Rogan with Nina Teicholz
recommendations.context: Teicholz on Rogan, walking through the case of The Big Fat Surprise.
recommendations.reason: An accessible long-form gateway to her case against the saturated-fat orthodoxy.

recommendations.item: The perfect treatment for diabetes and weight loss
recommendations.creator: Diet Doctor with Jason Fung
recommendations.context: Fung interviewed by Diet Doctor.
recommendations.reason: Linked specifically to back up the claim that 'small frequent meals' is bad advice — every time you eat, insulin spikes; the more spikes, the closer you get to insulin resistance.

recommendations.item: Caste, Capitalism and Chandra Bhan Prasad (Episode 296, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Chandra Bhan Prasad
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with the Dalit scholar Chandra Bhan Prasad.
recommendations.reason: Source of the poignant reframe — that Prasad's heart fills with pride seeing his village elders obese and diabetic, because their forebears could not have been prosperous enough to be either. Also of his counterintuitive read of Dalit women wearing the ghunghat at weddings.

recommendations.creator: Paul Graham
recommendations.context: Graham's framework for the four kinds of thinkers in any society.
recommendations.reason: Used here to identify the second source of pushback against new nutrition science — 'the aggressively conventional minded' who police received wisdom they have not actually examined.

recommendations.context: Nutritionist and physical trainer, also featured on The Seen and the Unseen episode 289.
recommendations.reason: Customised the protocol for Amit's body, goals and lifestyle. Specialises in keto for vegetarians (rare expertise). Source of the insight that multivitamins are useless — like a five-star buffet that meets no daily requirement; better to identify deficiencies and dose B12, E, C separately.

recommendations.item: Shruti Jahagirdar is the Sporty One (Episode 289, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Jahagirdar
recommendations.context: Amit's deep-dive episode with Shruti Jahagirdar.
recommendations.reason: Background on Amit's nutritionist and physical trainer — a window into her thinking before consulting her.

recommendations.creator: Coomi Kapoor
recommendations.context: A personal-historical account of India's 1975-77 Emergency by a journalist whose own husband was jailed at the time.
recommendations.reason: An important reminder that democracy is not given. Half the opposition was in jail, hordes of journalists were jailed, and as Advani put it, 'they were asked to bend, they chose to crawl.' Kapoor was on Amit's podcast (TSATU 305); pairs with Gyan Prakash's TSATU 103 on the Emergency as not an aberration but built into the centralising DNA of the Indian state.

recommendations.item: Coomi Kapoor Has the Inside Track (Episode 305, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Coomi Kapoor
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with the journalist Coomi Kapoor.
recommendations.reason: The conversation that surfaced the lived texture of the Emergency, accompanying her book.

recommendations.item: Gyan Prakash on the Emergency (Episode 103, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Gyan Prakash
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with the historian Gyan Prakash.
recommendations.reason: Argues the Emergency was not aberrant — the centralisation was already in the constitution and the state's DNA, inheriting from the colonial state.

recommendations.creator: Abbott Labs
recommendations.context: A wearable continuous glucose monitor (sensor + reader) that lasts two weeks per patch.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's primary recommendation — and the tool at the heart of this episode — for running a two-to-three-month research project on yourself, once a year, to fix lifelong food habits. With a humble plea to Abbott to open the API so an open-source app can pipe readings into a Google Sheet. Practical wisdom: stick the patch in but wait a full 24 hours before initialising it, and do a couple of days of finger-prick calibration.

recommendations.item: Lenin's Tomb: The Last Days of the Soviet Empire
recommendations.creator: David Remnick
recommendations.context: Remnick's book on the dying days of the USSR, written when he was Moscow correspondent for the Washington Post; he later became editor of The New Yorker.
recommendations.reason: A great narrative about how a society struggles with itself in dealing with an authoritarian state, and how the possibilities for progress are damaged for a very long time. Doubly interesting today because we know what Remnick didn't — that Russia was about to slide back to hell under Putin. As Gordon Brown said, the rule of law is a difficult project for the first 500 years.

recommendations.item: The Bridge: The Life and Rise of Barack Obama
recommendations.creator: David Remnick
recommendations.context: Remnick's biography of Obama.
recommendations.reason: Mentioned as another Remnick gem, and the source of Amit's poker-trivia favourite — that Obama played poker in the late 1990s not for the game or the money but because it was the best way to socialise and network with Democratic insiders in a relaxed, convivial setting.

recommendations.item: Host-diet-gut microbiome interactions influence human energy balance
recommendations.creator: Karen D. Corbin et al., Nature Communications, June 2023
recommendations.context: A meticulous experimental paper measuring downstream metabolism of identical-calorie simple-carb vs complex-carb diets.
recommendations.reason: The study Ajay leans on for the 200-calorie-a-day 'discount' from eating complex carbs — simple carbs are absorbed before they can reach the gut microbiome (which shrivels), while complex carbs feed the microbiome 8x more activity, and the microbes themselves consume some of the energy. A calorie is not a calorie.

recommendations.item: Are all calories created equal? Your gut microbes don't think so.
recommendations.creator: Anahad O'Connor, The Washington Post
recommendations.context: A popular write-up of the Corbin et al. paper.
recommendations.reason: Accessible journalistic version of the gut-microbiome calorimetry findings.

recommendations.creator: Louis C.K.
recommendations.context: Louis C.K.'s television series.
recommendations.reason: Source of the 'bang bang' bit — eating a complete meal at one restaurant, walking out, and immediately eating another complete meal of a different cuisine at the next. Amit's COVID-era biryani-plus-pizza days qualify.

recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier appearance in which Ajay laid out the analogy between root-microbiome starvation in hydroponic plants and gut-microbiome starvation in humans on simple carbs.
recommendations.reason: Background to the conceptual bridge Ajay draws here: feeding chemical fertilizer to plants makes them mean to their root microbiome; feeding simple carbs to ourselves makes us mean to our gut microbiome.

core_ideas.concept: Sugar Is Uniquely Addictive — and Hidden
core_ideas.explanation: Sugar hits the reward centre of the brain like nicotine or alcohol, but unlike coffee (jitters) or alcohol (hangover) it gives no warning sign of overconsumption. We never realise we're addicted because we are never without it long enough to feel withdrawal. Taubes-via-Pollan's haunting illustration: a child's first taste of cake icing is not pleasure but ecstasy in the literal sense — 'beside himself, no longer here with me in space and time.'
core_ideas.quote: We don't realize we are addicted. We will never experience a withdrawal symptom because we are never without sugar for long enough.

core_ideas.explanation: Until 1913, cigarette smoke was alkaline — try to inhale it and you cough. In 1913 the new Camel brand increased the carbohydrate (sugar) content of the tobacco, which turned the smoke acidic and easy to inhale. Sugar literally enabled the modern addictive cigarette. In a strong sense, sugars enabled smoking to cause lung cancer.
core_ideas.quote: In a sense, sugars enabled smoking to cause lung cancer.

core_ideas.concept: Ancel Keys and the Cherry-Picked Seven Countries
core_ideas.explanation: Ancel Keys's famous late-1950s Seven Countries Study purported to show saturated fat caused heart disease. He picked the seven countries where the data fit; he excluded France, Switzerland, Germany — high-fat-low-heart-disease places that would have falsified him. The American Heart Association argued against him in 1957; by 1960 he was running the AHA panel. By 1961 the official guideline was low-fat. By the 1980s the obesity epidemic was off to the races. Falsifiability matters — and when a charismatic researcher refuses it, an entire civilisation can pay for forty years.
core_ideas.quote: If you take the route of falsifiability, you have to examine anything that could disprove your hypothesis.

core_ideas.concept: The Sugar Lobby Was Stronger Than FDR
core_ideas.explanation: Franklin Roosevelt called the sugar lobby the most powerful interest group he had encountered. The lobby funded compliant academic studies, suppressed dissent (Reader's Digest spiked Jean Mayer's 1976 New York Times piece after a phone call to the editor), and made critics feel they had 'desecrated the American flag.' The man who won World War II in some sense couldn't beat the sugar lobby.
core_ideas.quote: This is a man who won World War II in a sense, but couldn't beat the sugar lobby.

core_ideas.concept: A Calorie Is Not a Calorie
core_ideas.explanation: A calorie measured in a calorimeter — burning food in pure oxygen — is not the same as a calorie metabolised by the human body. A hundred calories of sugar spikes insulin and stores fat; a hundred calories of complex carbs feeds the gut microbiome (which itself consumes some of the energy); a hundred calories of fat does neither. Macronutrients differ in their hormonal and microbial fates. The calorie-in/calorie-out model collapses on contact with biology.
core_ideas.quote: A calorie burned in a calorimeter is not the same as a calorie metabolised by the human body.

core_ideas.concept: White Rice and Maida Are One Reaction From Sugar
core_ideas.explanation: White flour (maida) and white rice are merely polymerised sugar — one reaction by an enzyme called amylase away from glucose. Nutritionally, 100 g of white rice is essentially equivalent to 100 g of sugar. We have culturally normalised these things; once you see them on a CGM 'there's really no peace you can make' with them.
core_ideas.quote: These simple starches, the white flour and the white rice, are merely polymerized sugars — they are one reaction away from becoming sugar.

core_ideas.concept: The Continuous Glucose Monitor Is the Key Tool of Self-Knowledge
core_ideas.explanation: HbA1c is a smeared three-month average; the CGM is a real-time instrument. The objective is not just lowering a single number but staying inside a target band — say 70 to 160 mg/dL — for over 80% of the day, with low volatility and no surges. The CGM is also expensive, but you don't need it always: do two-to-three rigorous months once a year (the behavioural-economics window for habit formation), build a baseline, then run with it.

Carbs on an empty stomach hit the blood almost like an injection. Fibre first, then protein and fat, then carbs gets the body busy on slow-to-digest material first, so by the time the carbs arrive the absorption is gentle. The traditional Western meal order — salad, then main, then dessert — turns out to be ideal. Even ice cream eaten last after a real meal is not the catastrophe the same ice cream is mid-afternoon on its own.
core_ideas.quote: The order in which you eat food matters.

core_ideas.explanation: Sugar is not sugar. Identical doses of sugar produce different surges depending on companions: sugar alone, sugar with fat, sugar with fat plus glycaemic-index-suppressing spices (ginger, nutmeg, cinnamon). Each generates a visibly different CGM curve. Hence the weirdly defensible position that 'if you must eat sugar, eat ice cream — preferably ice cream laced with ginger, nutmeg, and cinnamon.'
core_ideas.quote: Sugar is not sugar; it matters what it goes with.

core_ideas.concept: Insulin Resistance and the Case for Fasting
core_ideas.explanation: Every time you eat, especially carbs, insulin spikes. The more frequent the spikes, the more the body slides toward insulin resistance and eventually diabetes. The fix is two-pronged: lower the frequency (intermittent fasting; for Amit, one meal a day) and lower the intensity (low-carb). 'Small frequent meals' is therefore exactly the wrong advice. There is a reason every major religion built fasting into its calendar.
core_ideas.quote: There is a reason in a sense why fasting was a part of every major religion.

core_ideas.concept: Gut Microbiome and the Hydroponics Analogy
core_ideas.explanation: Plants fed simple chemical fertiliser become mean to their root microbiome — they underinvest in feeding it, and the plant suffers. The same dynamic plays out in humans: simple carbs are absorbed before they can reach the gut microbiome, which shrivels; complex carbs reach the microbiome, generating 8x more activity. The microbes themselves consume some of the energy, so eating the same calories as complex rather than simple carbs gives a roughly 200-calorie-a-day discount (Corbin et al., Nature Communications, 2023). A calorie is not a calorie, again.
core_ideas.quote: Those blokes don't do it for free. They consume some of the energy themselves.

core_ideas.explanation: Eating dietary cholesterol — egg yolks, fatty meats — has essentially no relationship to blood cholesterol levels. The body tightly regulates cholesterol synthesis. Time magazine's covers tell the cultural story: cholesterol is bad / cholesterol is fine / butter is back. Egg yolks may be among the healthiest foods known to humans; up to 25 a day is safe by sources Amit cites.
core_ideas.quote: Have all the egg yolk you want.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's reframing of the embarrassed-doctor moment: in non-communicable diseases, doctors are amateur psychologists. They are reading your discipline and your character and tailoring advice to what they think you'll actually do. If they think you can't hack lifestyle change, they'll just drug the hell out of you. This is rational behaviour — but it means the same diagnosis yields totally different treatments depending on who the doctor thinks you are.
core_ideas.quote: If they think that you're really not gonna be able to execute lifestyle changes, then they'll figure that I'm just going to drug the hell out of you.

core_ideas.concept: Food Is a Social Experience — Change Your Tribe
core_ideas.explanation: If a cheesecake is in the fridge, it ends up inside you. So the change has to happen at the point of purchase, and that means changing the conversation with the people you live and eat with. It is acceptable — actually advisable — to be 'rude' and reshape the food landscape around you. Diet alone is solitary; food is communal. The hard work is the social negotiation.
core_ideas.quote: If there is a cheesecake in the fridge it would be inside you.

core_ideas.explanation: The answer is not to follow Atkins, or keto, or any prescribed plan as a dogma. The right move is to ask: what are my preferences, my food culture, my tastes — and how do I adapt them so my body responds well? There is no one fixed answer, because different people are different. The CGM enables this DIY culture; it makes the experiment cheap and personal.

Diabetes rises with prosperity in some countries (India, USA) but not in others (Japan, France, Germany). Pure income elasticity does not explain the obesity epidemic — the cultural variable (which sweet foods become normalised, which interest groups dominate, which dietary guidelines get codified) matters. Chandra Bhan Prasad makes the inverse, poignant point: that his village elders are now obese and diabetic, which a generation ago they could not have afforded to be.

core_ideas.concept: Three Sources of Pushback on New Nutrition Science
core_ideas.explanation: The same dogma persists today because of three forces: (1) corporate interest groups — every processed food pushing 'no added sugar' labels that hide sugar in other forms; (2) the aggressively conventional minded (Paul Graham) — people who police received wisdom; (3) the lag in medical training — any doctor who graduated even circa 2010 was likely trained in the wrong nutrition, and only those who keep updating themselves are reliable.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: On naming: 'We thought we could call this show Amit and Shah, because, you know, Amit and Shah. But we're not gonna do that.'

On the cheesecake problem: Ajay — 'If there is a cheesecake in the fridge it would be inside you.' Amit — 'But if there is a choice of the cheesecake being inside you and you being inside the cheesecake, please choose the second option. Even if it is hard to imagine and a little bit messy and you'll need a good shower later.'
On apple juice as concealed sugar: 'I feel jealous of apple juice — that kind of apple juice — because I find it so hard to stay concentrated.'
Amit's chess as a brain-fog meter: his rating drops 150 points after a pizza, more after biryani-plus-pizza. Tracked, in earnest, on chess.com under a pseudonym.
Ajay on poker: 'You avoid sugar but you get gambling. I don't know which is a bigger evil.' Amit's reply: 'I didn't get type 2 diabetes by playing poker, so we know what the answer to that is.'

Amit's pitch: shirts. 'I've been saying to people, like guys, gift me shirts.' Producer Vartika has decreed that he needs patterned shirts; he's down to plain white only. So: like, subscribe, donate a shirt.
Michael Pollan calling Gary Taubes 'a Solzhenitsyn of the nutrition world' — likening him to the dissident who exposed the Soviet gulags.
Pollan in Botany of Desire on his son Isaac's first cake icing: 'an ecstasy in the literal sense of that word — beside himself with the pleasure of it, no longer here with me in space and time.'
Sidney Mintz in Sweetness and Power: 'Sugars, particularly highly refined sucrose, produce peculiar physiological effects.'

Roy Kulash Chandar Bose, 1907 (a Bengali proto-physician): 'There is not the slightest shadow of a doubt that with the progress of civilization, of high education and increased wealth and prosperity of the people under the British rule, the number of diabetic cases has enormously increased.'

Elliott Joslin, the prominent early-20th-century American diabetes physician, in 1925: 'Automobiles cause diabetes' (people stopped walking, got fat, got diabetes — so the obesity link was already half-seen, but he absolved sugar).

Researcher David Kritchevsky, on the heat that came down on anyone challenging the saturated-fat consensus: 'We were jumped on. People would just spit on us. It's hard to imagine now the heat of the passion. It was just like we had desecrated the American flag.'
Franklin Roosevelt calling the sugar lobby the most powerful interest group he had ever seen — invoked as the man who won World War II in a sense but couldn't beat the sugar lobby.
Louis C.K.'s 'bang bang' from his show Louie: walk into a restaurant, eat a complete meal, walk out, walk into a different restaurant, eat another complete meal.

Paul Graham's 'aggressively conventional minded' from The Four Quadrants of Conformism — the people who police received wisdom they have not actually examined; one of the three sources of resistance to new nutrition science.
L.K. Advani on the Indian press during the Emergency: 'They were asked to bend, they chose to crawl.'
Gordon Brown: 'The rule of law is a difficult project for the first 500 years' — invoked to explain why post-Soviet Russia slid back to authoritarianism.

Trivia from David Remnick's The Bridge: Barack Obama played poker in the late 1990s — not for love of the game or the money, but because it was the best way to socialise and network with Democratic insiders in a relaxed, convivial setting.

Chandra Bhan Prasad, on visiting his village: his heart fills with pride seeing the elders obese and diabetic, because two generations ago they could not have been prosperous enough to be either. (And his counterintuitive read of a Dalit woman wearing the ghunghat at her wedding as exercising a choice she couldn't earlier.)
